utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic. I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Nikolic for the Beara team which therefore is not represented as yet this morning. Is Mr. Lazarevic here? Yes, okay. And then I don't see any other absences from the Defence. Prosecution is just Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Beara, we waited seven minutes to see if your lawyers were turning up or not and we have got no news so we had to start. However, you have a right not to have the proceedings continue in the absence of your lawyers. There has been no explanation from them, although some of my staff is trying to contact them. You can also waive this right that I have just mentioned, which would mean that we can proceed in their absence and eventually hopefully they will turn up. What is your choice? THE ACCUSED BEARA: [Interpretation] Yes, I think we can continue with the proceedings. They will probably come soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Beara. We are also sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this morning for the first session. That's because our colleague Judge Stole is busy with something urgent that has come up and he will be with us after the first break. Official business is what I mean. And I understand there are some preliminaries, no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that your preliminary was in relation to the Beara motions in any case, Mr. McCloskey, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And given that, it's probably more productive to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right. That's what we were going to suggest in any case. So thank you and let's bring in Colonel Vuga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Dobar dan, Gospodine Vuga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony today. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vuga. I will continue where we left off, but before we do that, could you please take your report, because we'll take another tack now. Your report is the first document in your binder, so take it out, please. And we will start with point -- with 3.4, with paragraph 3.4 in your report. It's 1D1175, page 29 in B/C/S, and page 34 in English. In this part of your report, you wrote about threats to security in the area of the Drina Corps pending the establishment of UNPAs in Srebrenica and Zepa. Could you please tell us, in light of the facts you presented in your report, to briefly describe the situation in this area just before the UNPAs were established?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the UNPAs were established, in the area of the Drina Corps, the security situation was rather complex, inasmuch as various activities were taking place. Operations were conducted on a large scale, and there were many of them. Those operations posed a threat to the population, to certain features and installations, and completely disrupted life in that area. That would be most briefly. The operations themselves are listed in the report and they tell us that the situation required certain measures to be taken for normalcy to be restored. These actions and operations were variegated from incursions of sabotage and terrorist groups to actions by paramilitaries of the then-still-unrecognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that the consequences of these actions in some locations were catastrophic, disastrous. In one part of that area, around 30 Serb villages were almost completely destroyed and evacuated. Around 10 villages remained around Bratunac and Srebrenica that were still holding out, that were not yet destroyed. A later attack targeted even those villages, leaving five ethnically pure Serb villages that were not evacuated and destroyed. The destruction was not justified by military need. It was instead a result of well-thought-out activity aimed at maximising the damage to that area. A specific feature of all this was that the method of destruction was relentless and undiscriminating. In Srebrenica itself, very serious problems occurred, and there was total disruption to the security of the Serb population. And that manifested itself specifically and particularly in the killing of Zoran Zekic, an MP in the assembly and the president of the SDS in Srebrenica. After that, there occurred a massive departure of the Serb population from Srebrenica. The killings and ambushes that were set up caused great fear and sowed panic amongst people because they thought it was not safe to move around any more or to even stay there and that resulted later in many other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I let you see the judgement in the Naser Oric case and you had occasion to read it in that judgement. You saw that some of those attacks on Serb villages were noted. But tell me, if you remember, who was designated as the source of those attacks? Which groups?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the groups that acted from Srebrenica against the surrounding area but primarily it was paramilitary units that were organised locally. That is their basic characteristic, that they were organised locally. They originated from that area and they were active in that area. They participated in the internal conflict in that region and the point of that activity was to inflict great damage and losses. That is why these units were organised and they were active in that area where they stayed and where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to our two decisions on adjudicated facts, one very recent, following a motion that you yourself filed, the other one in the early stages of the trial that deals precisely with the events that your questioning the witness about. We wouldn't like to have repetitions. In other words, you already have these adjudicated facts, and in addition, if you also look at the decision on the agreed facts, you also find repetitive concessions from the Prosecution that during the 1993-19 95 period, when Srebrenica and Zepa were declared protected enclaves, there were these incursions. So if we could speed up on this issue and move on to your next area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vuga, you have seen that it is emphasised in these decisions that civilians also took part in those attacks.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is noted in those decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now about the security aspects that occurred as a result of these attacks which were mounted not only by paramilitary units but also by civilians in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's too vague. We need a time frame for that in order it to be relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and connect with the Judge's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a fair comment, Mr. Zivanovic. If you could be more specific as to which period of time you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For whole time we referred to the period before the establishment of safe areas. It means from the beginning of the war in Bosnia in April 1992 until the April 1993, when safe areas were established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The security aspect of the involvement of civilians or massive involvement of civilians, outside any military units, added on to the threat and it became a general threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, for the record, the Chamber notes that Mr. Ostojic entered the courtroom at 9.22. Mr. Ostojic, we have started and continued the sitting after having asked your client if he waived his right, which he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President and Your Honours. I sincerely apologise to the Court, the counsel, the accused, the Prosecution and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this part of your report you stated that only in 1992, 376 actions took place. Could we look at 1D1283, please? It's in your third binder.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it. 1D?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did take into account this document when you wrote your report. What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents the total number of actions, the time when they occurred, the units involved and the nature of attacks. We can see that these are hamlets, small towns and villages, and we can see which village or hamlet was targeted by attacks in the relevant period, and we can also see the total number of these attacks, and we can see that the attacks were almost daily. Sometimes we have more than one attack in one day. There was not a single quiet day in this whole area throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document records all combat actions in this area from 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is -- this is leading. He's just going over his report on the screen, it's always going to be leading. This person should not need his report in front of him to testify. This seems to me to be right in the heart of the area that really isn't part of -- contested part of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This is what I tried to explain to Mr. Zivanovic, who, however, seems to ignore what I have stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we are all in agreement here. You don't need to dwell on these events. Please move on to your next topic. And obviously, if -- with this understanding, because last thing we would want to do is not to be fair. If at any time this chapter of events is opened by the Prosecution, then we will reopen all doors to you, but in the meantime, please go ahead. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to reiterate, the Prosecution agrees there were plenty of good and legitimate reasons for the VRS to attack Srebrenica in July 1995 and that there were also some that, as you know, were part of the Prosecution's case were not and that a mixed motive situation is what we have here. I do not disagree that there were plenty of legitimate reasons for this attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They have been established by this Tribunal as well. So let's move to your next item.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just ask the witness how many victims, Serbian victims, fell in this period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, if you know, in this period, before the UNPA was established, how many Serb people fell victim to these attacks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documentation I had, 2.100 people fell victim to these attacks before the UNPA was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D1162?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- for interrupting. The CLSS version of the final report is not in e-court. This is apparently a draft that's in e-court and we will be objecting to anything, that a draft comes in, so if you could fix that, we would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Do you want to consult with your assistant?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I must consult to see what -- the final version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest while you are consulting, you switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you right now anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But keep in mind the words of Mr. McCloskey, that you otherwise have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, please. Does the witness know out of these 2.100, how many were military and how many were civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, when you look at this list, do you know how many people were soldiers and how many were civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no classification in the list, not of that sort. You could only look at the years of birth and try and guess who members of the military formations were. I did not do that because I did not have the relevant data that would enable me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, we come to the period that concerns the establishment of the protected area, of which you spoke on page 31 of the B/C/S version, or page 36 of the English version of your report. I'm not going to ask you to look at the document of the Security Council of the United Nations establishing the protected areas or the disarmament agreement. We have seen all these more than once. My question to you is this: What was the position of the warring parties regarding the disarming or the implementation of the disarmament agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position of the warring parties contradicted each other. The Serbian side, on the same day, on the 18th of April, issued an order which served as the foundation for the implementation of the agreement, whereas on the Muslim side, an order was issued to the effect that the agreement should not be complied with and that the arms should be kept, and the rest is history.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find this position in any of the documents that were available to you or in any other source?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first position can be found in the order of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska issued on the 18th of April 1993. That's the Serbian position. As for the Muslim position, I found that in the book by Sefer Halilovic entitled, "Crafty Strategy," who spoke about his actions from the moment he signed the agreement onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now please look 1D7221.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D721.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at page 3 in B/C/S and page 2 in the English version of this book? In the B/C/S version, it can be found in the penultimate paragraph, the penultimate sentence as well, and in the English translation it is the last paragraph at the bottom of the page. Tell me, please -- could we please look at 1D1285? I believe that this is one of the documents that you have already spoken about. Could you please tell us something about the details of this document? What did the Serb side order thereby? Who issued the order and what is the order about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, on the 18th of April 1993, on the day when the agreement was signed, sent an order which referred to the cease-fire and the actions regarding Srebrenica. This was delivered to the Drina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps and the order outlines details of the cease-fire, the actions to be executed during the cease-fire, and what actions are to be expected and carried out in the forthcoming period. Everybody was duty-bound to carry out the order and implement it because the protected areas of Zepa, Srebrenica and Gorazde were in their area of responsibility, and it also said in the order that some actions will be carried out according to the agreement but that they would be carried out in the forthcoming period. The agreement was not very precise. It lacked some details. And that's why the second agreement was signed. It should have provided more details about the actions. However, this order enabled the implementation of the second agreement and the conditions that it would contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you this. We know that this agreement was not implemented and there is no dispute about the fact that the demilitarisation was not carried out, and I will not dwell upon these issues. Can you tell me, however, whether you were able to establish how many Serbs were killed during the existence of the enclave, i.e. from the establishment of the protected area to its fall on the 11th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I analysed the list that was submitted to me, I established, based on the times of death, that in 1993, which was the first year, 594 Serb victims fell, 594 Serbs were killed. Obviously, I can't give you the date. The agreement was signed on the 18th of April and one can conclude that most of that happened because the month of April was one-third of the year and 594 people were killed in that year, after the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you establish how many victims fell later on, in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second piece of information is more reliable because during those years the area existed continuously. In 1994 and in 1995, until the moment the protected area was abolished after the events that happened, there were another 591 victims in the area. So this was in -- during the time when the area was completely functional as a protected area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was confirmed. Let me just make sure that you established the number of these victims from the same list that I've already shown you, which was 1D1162.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to establish that from that list. I looked at the list, and looking at the times when they were killed, I could establish how many were killed in 1993, 1994 and 1995, and I analysed this but I separated the year 1993 to show that the protected area did not exist throughout the whole year but in looking at the dates and times of death, you can see that the number of victims continued to grow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The list depicts the year when these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. This is depicted in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that these facts are also confirmed by some other documents testifying to the attacks against the Serbs while the protected area existed. Could you please give us the title of some of these documents, if you can remember them off the cuff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a document which shows that during the functioning of the protected area, about the actions of the sabotage units. The command of the 28th Division sent its report to the command of the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, which speaks about the fact of the Muslim people and about several sabotage and terrorist actions carried out by groups from Srebrenica and it also lists casualties and damage inflicted on the Serbs in the area and on the Serb forces. And the figure that is mentioned there is 70 members of the Republika Srpska army. So this is a very strong form of action or influence against the environment. In an order that was issued in June 1994, it says, and it was issued by the Army of Republika Srpska, but then abolished the 18th of April order. It is mentioned that attacks were being carried out from the protected area against the local population and the units of Army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, this order confirms that the actions continued and that there was not enough control of the zone in terms of its demilitarisation. So these would be the documents that speak about the victims that fell even after the protected area was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you also speak about the planning of some major actions, not only sabotage and terrorist actions. I'm talking about item 3.20 in your report. And you mention also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the non-specificity. They seem to be equating sabotage actions which are -- and terrorist actions as being the same and that soldiers that die as victims. So if we could be clearer on our language, because that, I don't think it equates with the reality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, taking note of what Mr. McCloskey said, would you like to rephrase the question, which you haven't finished in any case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the nature of the actions that you speak about and that were carried out from the enclaves against the targets in the Serbian villages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that this is due to the translation and due to the context of the protected area. This is not combat activity. This is sabotage actions from the protected areas, and this was the nature of these attacks. This was not a regular combat. I looked at the protected area, its nature and actions that were carried out from there. There was no combat there. Combat had been discontinued and no combat activity could take place in view of the agreement that had been reached. One has to say that these were sabotage and terrorist actions that were launched from the protected areas and not regular combat activities that were taking place. These were impossible, because the agreement was in place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to mention that the witness said two times "terrorist," the word "terrorist" action, but they were not in record. Actually, he mentioned this word after "sabotage," after the word "sabotage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can see it on line 21 at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but two times before that he mentioned the word "terrorist."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I would assume line 16, I would assume line 16, but let's move. Let's move, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to these actions, were some other military actions of a larger scale prepared while the protected area existed in Srebrenica? Was anything prepared from that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A major action was being prepared and the aim was to establish corridors between the zones of Zepa, Gorazde, and Srebrenica, so that these three might be connected with the territory under the control of the Muslim forces. Later on, in the further stage of these activities, they would have been enlarged until the moment they could be liberated. This was the main idea behind the actions. So there would have been final liberation of the temporarily occupied territories which meant the territories that were at the time under the Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at document 1D740? Can you tell me, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us now who wrote this document and to whom is it addressed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written in the staff of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is sent to the command of the 8th Operative Group, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document designate the territories that were to be the target of the planned action?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was an idea from the commander of the 8th Operation Group, Naser Oric. It was later verified, and analysed, pointing out the risks involved, but they still decided to proceed with preparation and implementation. The territories are designated and the axes along which corridors were to be established, and later on, activities were to continue along the lines that I already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in order to execute such an action and all the other actions that were planned, whether the forces in the enclave had enough manpower, equipment, weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when this idea was launched, the forces in the enclave were still not sufficiently organised. Prior to that, they were recognised and they were reorganised, from the 8th Operation Group, the 28th Division was established, and that resulted in a new approach to this whole operation. Of course, they were not to act alone. They were to act in coordinated action with the forces of the 2nd Corps of the BH army along the axes indicated. But at that time those forces were in the process of being organised precisely for tasks and missions of this type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if any actions were launched in this period to arm the enclave in order to mount larger-scale military operations, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the reorganisation of units in Srebrenica, without additional arms supply, would not result in a force sufficient for such a large-scale operation. It was organised to -- air drops of arms were organised so that the units in Srebrenica could perform all the other preparations, including primarily the training of men to use the weapons supplied. That was done, and there exists an analysis that provides rather reliable information on how much weaponry was supplied to Srebrenica, and the analysis ends with the note that Sarajevo even did not have that amount of weapons to defend itself in 1992-1993. They had less weapons than Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at document 1D744?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This document bears two different dates, two different years. I see the 17th of February 1996 in the header, and a bit lower down, 17th February 1995. Could you just tell me -- I believe this document contains a table on page 9. You see these amounts in the bottom right corner. Can you tell us exactly what it means, UBS, 10 T and MTS, 5 T?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are totals of lethal combat material, 10 tonnes, and materiel and equipment, 5 tonnes. Those -- this is different materiel, in terms of purpose, but all this served to equip and arm the 28th Division. It means that this amount of materiel was delivered by air to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We see from this that it was before March, that is before the establishment of the UNPA. Can we now move on to the next page? Before March 1993. Let us look at the amounts delivered later.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one section referring to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean on the previous page? I didn't see that. Can we move back to the previous page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that page, in number 8, we see 20th March 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page. Can you see here how much equipment was shipped?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are flights to Zepa. 17 tonnes of lethal materiel was delivered and 6 tonnes of materiel and equipment. We see 26 passengers. I have nothing more to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, you have studied quite a few documents about materiel and equipment and lethal materiel delivered to Srebrenica and Zepa. Have you seen even one document whereby the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to deliver food or medicine to their troops in these areas?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not found a single document that could indicate that Srebrenica and Zepa were supplied with food and other things the army needed, except combat equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at 1D745? You recall this document, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember this. I'd like you to focus on page 6. What kind of document is this? I forgot to ask you that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This discrepancy in dates tells us something about the time this document was drafted. The previous analysis was presented to the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the way army General Rasim Delic thought convenient. He describes these activities and qualifies the nature of these activities in the conclusion. He describes all the things that were done for the protected areas Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde to be militarily enabled as opposed to what has been done in connection with the agreement. This rationale was presented when the assembly was familiarised with this analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 2 on page 6, only the second sentence, which says, "What can we say about resistance if even with so many anti-armour weapons, not a single tank was destroyed?" Can you tell us what are anti-armour resources?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were guided anti-armour missiles that Srebrenica was supplied with. But I would like to highlight another aspect here that is very important in my view. This is an assessment of how the equipment was used, not the lack of equipment or the deficiencies of that equipment. What is important is that there is no answer to the question why the equipment provided was not adequately used, as had been expected and planned. In fact, there is no answer to the question whether Srebrenica was militarily captured or was lost by its defenders in some other way. That is, in fact, the dilemma that Rasim Delic presented to the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify one more thing? This anti-armour equipment, is it considered to be heavy or light weaponry, if you know of course?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it is classified. I know this equipment but I'm an air force man and I cannot tell you about how it is classified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to June 1995. It is reflected in your report in para 3.30. You wrote there about one order of the 2nd Corps. I would like you to tell us what kind of order that was. I will give you the number of the exhibit in a moment. 1D946. It seems that this document has not been translated, so tell us briefly what does it deal with, because you refer to it in your report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to this order because, on the 17th of June 1995, that is 15 days or so before Krivaja 95, the 28th Division was ordered to carry out preparations to launch an offensive, and the order says that all these preparations need to be carried out in order to stretch thin and inflict damage upon aggressor forces, and there is a section that refers to Zepa in case of an attack mounted from Zepa. It was an effort to tie up and stretch the Serb forces in this area as thin as possible so that combat activities in other areas could be affected more efficiently because it was difficult, because it would have been difficult for the VRS to get reinforcements. It was a synchronised operation with comprehensive actions throughout the region, discloses the real nature of Srebrenica as an area where an army was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document mention coordinated action with any other element? And if so, which?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that it was to be a synchronised operation, which means that the moment of attack, the time of attack, would be determined later, but preparations were aimed at preparing the forces, that everything that needs to be done be done and that the capacities of the 28th Division would be evaluated correctly so that they would not be threatened and the activities of the UNPA would not be compromised. They wanted to avoid compromising the UNPAs as a basis for these activities of forces organised in this way. This was a preparation for what was to come later, that is a combat operation launched by these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were looking at all the documents dated after the 17th of July 1995, the documents of the BiH army, did you find any trace of actions being carried out pursuant to this order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, what is written in the reports about the sabotage and terrorist actions that were carried out from the area, and the reports were sent to the command of the 2nd Corps, coincides with the preparatory order and the future actions that were to ensue. This is a report on the contribution of the forces in Srebrenica to the fight of the Muslim people. This is a short report showing what was done in the area with regard to what is stated herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, I also wanted to ask you this: In the documents that you perused, could you obtain any information as to whether the Bosnian authorities, i.e. the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, allowed the Muslim population or soldiers to leave the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa in the course of their existence up to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what I could see in the document that concerns the fate of a group from Zepa that had tried to leave Zepa and go to the territory under the control of the Muslim forces, measures were taken and it is clear that there was a ban imposed on the population in the protected areas to leave those protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have mentioned this report about the actions that were carried out. Let's please look at that report. Actually, we will look at it a little bit later. For the time being, let's look at the report dated 23 June 1995. This is 1D742. 1D742.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have it on the screen and I can follow it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just see whether it has been translated. I believe it has been. Could you please tell us, just briefly, what is this report related to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drafted on the 30th of June 1995, and it is a chronological overview of the actions that were carried out and the results thereof. I looked at the report from the security point of view, the security in the area of Srebrenica and its surroundings, and it has been established that this was a very grave form of threatening the safety of units and a violation of the status of the protected area. From the security point of view, this was a great warning about the status of safety around the area and the need to establish a system of protection that would prevent the things that had been happening up to then. Obviously, there were gaps through which these sabotage and terrorist units could pass through. While there was a lull in the combat activities during the cease-fire and during the existence of the protected area after the signing of the agreement, they could still achieve such effects and they could still inflict damage. Somewhere towards the end, there is a conclusion saying that 70 or around 70 members of the Army of Republika Srpska had been liquidated in this reporting period or the period that this report refers to. This is a rather convincing document portraying things as they were at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this was all happening in the area of defence of what corps or what unit?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The protected area of Srebrenica and the 28th Division were in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to 1D283. This is a list of combat activities of the 2nd Corps. Can we go immediately to page 11 in B/C/S or page 17 in the English translation? [In English] Sorry. [Interpretation] 1D1283. I apologise. I've given you the wrong pages. In B/C/S, it is page 17 and the English it is 25.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give us the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is ERN 618. I'm sure you'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is the sequential number on the list that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The sequential number 618. Could you please explain what this is about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about an attack on Visnjica, on the 25th of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please look at the following bullet point or the following sequential number which is 619?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Defence of Srebrenica operation which took place between 26th of June and 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 26th of June, was there an attack by the Army of Republika Srpska on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout all this time, there was a situation which was defined by the relationship which was described in the testimonies of the members of Dutch Battalion who said that Srebrenica was not attacked but that actions were carried out from Srebrenica that provoked the Serbian side to respond at the places where those actions were organised, and the Dutch Battalion members themselves say that they were between two fires but that they were at cross-fire and that they were threatened. There were no other activities. Srebrenica did not come under any other attack that would call for this type of action or reaction to them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you get that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, did you find anywhere else that this date was the beginning of the action on the part of the Muslim army and that this was something that is part of this fight for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at this preparatory order where this is mentioned, but there are no other documents that would point to such activities. There is just a reference to the corridors and there is also the order that followed after the preparatory order of the 2nd Corps of the BiH army that was sent to the command of the 28th Division in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. So let's have a 25-minute break. The time now is -- I don't have it here. Anyway, 10.25, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we'll deal with the other matter, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Ostojic, later on, all right? Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that the final version of translation was in e-court. The only difference is because the final version has no exhibit numbers, draft has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, before we move to the specific duties of deputy commander for security in the Drina Corps, I'm just going to show you one more document which is related to what we have just talked about. This is document 1D1295. You have seen this document. It hasn't been translated. It's handwritten, as we can see. Can we just move to page 4 right away so that we can see who drafted the document? Do you see? Can you read the name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name is legible. It's Ramiz Becirovic, major, acting commander of the land forces, 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to -- go back to page 1, please? I only wanted to ask you about two things from this document. I wanted to go to item number 4, paragraph numbered 4. It's on this page, fine. Can you see this first column, what does it indicate? Can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first column indicates the defence liberation unit which was the mainstay of the combat actions and that was the 28th Division of the land forces, took part in combat, 6.000, the commander Ramiz Becirovic, active officer, his pre-war rank. I cannot read that part. He was a reserve officer before the war. His rank was captain, and the rank during the combat operation was major.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move to page 2, please, and just look at paragraph 12 there. Can you please read out paragraph 12, nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Date of execution of combat actions, the 26th of June, until the 16th of July 1995, and it lasted or the combat actions went on for 21 days."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move to the part of your findings on page 35 in the B/C/S version and page 34 -- actually page 34 in the B/C/S version and page 41 in the English version. It's 1D1175, the document. And in your copy of the report, it's page 34, at least I think so. We are going to look at item 4.1. Let's look at the B/C/S version too. Mr. Vuga, first you told us, in the first part of this chapter, that the name of the military action was wrong, from the perspective of military terminology and military doctrine, so I would ask you now to please explain this view of yours.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the definition that was given in the documents and the qualification of the Krivaja 95 operation or action, I looked at the military terminology and looked up the form of action that would be described in a specific way and from the point of view of the forces that were engaged and the objective and the tasks that were set before the units who were executing the assignment, I came to the conclusion that the name "operation" is inconsistent with the nature of the combat action or the level and the organisational units and the forces participating and the objective, that they are inconsistent with this term. The objective that was set was to improve the tactical position of the units in the area or around the area in order to prevent further actions which were mentioned before, I don't want to repeat that, from the zone, and in order to establish a more effective control of the border area of the zone. But also to stop communications, physical links, between the protected area and -- between the protected areas of Zepa and Srebrenica, in both directions. So pursuant to that definition, operation, it could not have been an operation, that could not have been at the operation level because the forces that were executing the activity and the objectives and the tasks set do not have such a character. And in my opinion, also pursuant to what was actually happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your report something about the strength of the Drina Corps units at that time in July 1995. Can we now look at 1D379, please? This is in 4.2 of your report, in the B/C/S version, it's on the following page. And on the English, in the English copy, it's all ready. In item 4.2 of your report you mentioned the number of members and you referred to this document, in particular, and said that lesser forces were or fewer forces were engaged for this Krivaja 95 action. So I would like to ask you, if you can, to tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conclusions on it being a smaller force are based on two documents. The first document is the one that we are looking at now, which gives the strength of the Drina Corps in July 1995. The other document is the order for offensive combat actions or assault combat actions of operative number 1, where it says that the corps units continue to execute their defence assignments that they had been engaged on before, and I'm going to continue to use the term that is being used, "Operation," even though I would like to note that what I said in that respect still applies. So in reference to such strength and the size of the defence assignment, a smaller corps force could be engaged here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this part of your report, you go on to say something about the engagement of the security organs or, rather, the duties of the security organ which would arise from the preparation of an action like this, regardless of whether we refer to it as an action, operation, or some other name. Can you please tell us something about it briefly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- these forces dealt with the security aspect. The military aspect was entrusted to broader forces. What I was interested were the duties and the status of the security organs in respect of execution of their assignment, in terms of the units that were executing the defence, pursuant to the order, and the units overall participating in the Krivaja 95 action because, in a way, their engagements were divided. Before, it was more directed to the units and to a lesser degree to the area around Srebrenica because the situation was more stable. Now, suddenly, this whole thing changed and the security organs were issued new assignments in relation to the Krivaja 95 operation. So that was the aspect from which I viewed the engagement of the forces, because it had to do with the security organs from the perspective of their duties and responsibilities as far as general security measures were concerned within commands and as far as the counter-intelligence security was concerned that dealt with the activities of the units, their deployment and everything else relating to this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to move to the organisational and establishment composition of the security organs of the command of the Drina Corps, or actually I would like you to tell us what this organisation was supposed to be pursuant to regulations, what was the establishment force of the Drina Corps organ supposed to be in July 1995. So could we look at document D1296? In the original, this is on page 15 and the English translation -- in the English translation, it's on page 23. The heading is on the last line and then the actual paragraph begins on page 24. However, there are no numbers in the translation. The translation refers to the original document as far as numbers are concerned. The security section is in front of number 57 in the original version. So we have the composition of that sector there. In the English version, I think we would need to move to the next page, because on page 23 we only have the heading, "Security section," not the substance. It seems that there is a technical error, so there is no number 57 in the translation. I don't know how this happened. Even 58/1 is missing. I don't know if this is because of the page break or due to some other reason but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I would imagine it's because of the page break. Can we go back one page? You see you have it there, you have chief 57, 58 and 58/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vuga, I would like to ask you to tell us what according to establishment would be the composition of the security section of the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, I would like to clarify a term that is being used in two instances which are different. One is the organ bezbednost, the security organ, and the other one would be the Drina Corps security organ or the command security organ. The security organ in everyday terminology would be the authorised officer in the security organ who has certain authorities and by establishment is posted to a function where he performs his duties. The command security organ is an organisational establishment structure in the command entrusted with executing the tasks that are within its purview. So by leaving out the words, "command," when we are talking to security organs, we would maybe think that we are talking about an organ, but when we say "security organ," we mean the officer. But when we say command security organ we mean a body which is within the command which is in charge of or entrusted with security assignments which are part of its assigned duties. So now we could communicate without confusion about what a security organ is and what a command security organ is. I hope that I have managed to explain the difference clearly enough so that when we discuss security organs, we always know precisely what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have done that quite clearly, but quite quickly, so I would just like to ask you to slow down a little bit in your explanations.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you. I'm going to explain much more in my explanation and I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just now like to ask you to respond to the question that has to do with the establishment formation for the security organ.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we are speaking about the security organ of the command of the Drina Corps. The security organ of the Drina Corps command, by establishment, is called the security section. The security section of the Drina Corps command comprised -- its composition was given by establishment and we see it right here in front of us under number 57 and on. The section was headed by the chief of the section. He was a colonel by establishment. His deputy for counter-intelligence affairs would be the next person in line whose duties by establishment were within the section, and these duties were set down. His rank would be Lieutenant Colonel. The next assistant chief of the section would be the person in charge of security staff affairs. It's very important to note the names of these assistants because later, in the performance of its duties in the section, these assistants were considered as officers within the sectors of their duties, and you can see that this is somebody who is in charge of counter-intelligence affairs and a person in charge of security staff affairs. So you can already see the division of labour between throws who are working within the command and those who would be working in the section. Then we have three other establishment posts. These would be desk officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now move to next page of the B/C/S text? I believe we also need to move on to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 58/2, we see desk officer. We have three officers in this rubric, three desk officers in the section, who also have certain duties assigned to them within the section. They are mainly dealing with counter-intelligence affairs. We have an officer for military police, desk officer for military police. This is noteworthy because this officer is extremely important to the section chief when military police-related affairs are concerned, professional management and guidance, and some affairs related to equipping the military police, where the security administration was technically responsible for providing equipment. It was through the security administration that equipment was supplied and delivered to the military police to the extent it was possible to actually be done at that time. Then we have an administrative -- assistant administrative officer, operator-typist and a driver. So we have this number of officers with a structure of ranks determined by establishment. The general conclusion about this section is that it is a very well-developed structure which has a complement by ranks that indicates their job is to do very complex and very extensive security affairs. Otherwise, the complement would be different. This section would look different. I had occasion in the Yugoslav People's Army to elaborate on the work of intelligence officers at corps level and I know exactly what was the work-load of individuals. If there are only as many as we see in this section then their work-load would be very high, both in the units and in the area of the corps that they are covering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To make this clearer, out of these nine persons, do all of them deal with security matters or there are perhaps some who do not work strictly on security matters, although they are part of the section?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of these are authorised officers in the security section who have IDs of security officers and may apply methods of security organs based on the powers given them. Those are personal powers. That is powers vested in the persons that are not assignable to other persons or other security organs. All these officers, save for the assistant for security staff affairs, are security organs who are authorised to apply these methods of work and the desk officer for military police, because in the segment of their job that is related to crime, the officer in charge of military police participates in these jobs as an authorised officer in the security organ, whenever the military investigating judge entrusts him with such work. He has to be an authorised officer in the security organ. That is the composition and the method of work, speaking of individuals, whereas the section as a whole discharges the security function in the way it is regulated by the rule of service of the security organ under the guidance and command of the chief of the security section. So they are under the command of the chief. The chief gives them their assignments, he monitors their performance, and he reports to his own superior, the corps commander, on the work of the section. That is the security section of the Drina Corps command, from the viewpoint of establishment, the way establishment envisaged that it should be organised and that it should function.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Can you look at the last two items on the list? Are they also security officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I finished my previous answer with the desk officer for military police. The assistant administrative officer, operator-typist, is not an authorised officer, although he is working with the security section, and, of course, the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, compared to this prescribed situation, what was the actual complement of the security organ in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can hardly talk about a full complement. We can talk about the chief of the section and one civilian who was a technical clerk processing documents, and the other vacancies were not filled, and we could say that the chief of section was the whole section, as far as the actual functioning is concerned. In that sense, it is astounding to look at his work-load and what he was actually able to do in the area of the Drina Corps in view of all that was going on, not only according to establishment but looking at the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say there was another person, a technical assistant, who would that be in the establishment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 58/4, the administrative assistant, operator-typist. But even he did less than was envisaged by the establishment. It was a civilian who was doing as much as he was able to do. An assistant administrative officer, operator-typist, would be a more complex job because it implies available of certain technical resources. It doesn't matter where this technical resource would be used. It's important that it is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it follow from that that only one person dealt with all the security affairs in the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the actual complement, one person, the chief of the section, was both the authorised commanding officer in the security section authorised to apply methods of the security organ, and he was the chief for all the other affairs, fulfilling the duties of all these other people who were not actually there. This work had to be done because the work is dictated by needs, not by prescribed complement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that the security chief was able to issue orders, was able to command only over those persons who were employed in the very section, security section, of the command of the Drina Corps. Does it mean that he had command over just this one other person that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please move on to the Operation Krivaja 95 itself? It's P107, Prosecutor's Exhibit 107. In your report, it's in paragraph 4.22. It's on page 38 in your copy. We need the first page of this document. I believe this is page 2. First of all, look at the first paragraph of this document and try to see what were the security aspects, if you see any, what are the security problems highlighted in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the third item, we see, "in the past few days, especially active are Muslim forces from the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. They continue to infiltrate sabotage terrorist groups which are attacking unprotected villages." This is the reason why the security situation needed to be analysed as defined in the order itself. It is obvious that security problems had escalated and become extremely serious in the area of the corps and they were more pronounced in the protected area of Srebrenica than before. So that the security organ, which was involved, had to be involved in evaluating the security situation and had to propose measures. The security organ had to derive from this specific tasks for the period when this order had to be implemented. In addition, the operations being prepared were one more reason to ensure that units prepare safely and move into action with the adequate security support and counter-intelligence support. From this, we clearly see what problems and tasks were facing the security organ and what it had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the lower part of this paragraph? We see a description of the enemy, deployment of enemy military forces. From this document, can you see whether the Army of Republika Srpska had accurate information about the enemy at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska, judging by what we read in the order, was well-acquainted with the deployment of the enemy. It had good counter-intelligence about this and knew the exact disposition of enemy forces, which means that it was not in the dark as to who it was facing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on to the next page, paragraph 4? English page 3. What is the set objective of this action? It's in paras 1 and 2, in passages 1 and 2 of this paragraph, in fact. Can you make an assessment from this set objective what number of prisoners of war could be expected in the execution of this action?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said something about the name of this operation, and the scale of the operation as planned defines it in my opinion as a tactical action. In terms of the way it was to be achieved, we see that it was about repelling enemy forces towards the enclave and narrowing down the enclave and cutting off communications between Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves. The aim was to stop this communication and place this sector under complete control. The set objective and the planned scale gave no indication whatsoever that any significant number of enemy -- of the enemy could be taken prisoner because the objective was tactical, that is to reduce Srebrenica to the narrow urban zone. It was not about capturing enemy units. So there are no elements to conclude that there would be a large number of prisoners of war. On the contrary, all the elements indicate that only a small number of prisoners of war was expected. That was the evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now move on to the fifth page of this document? It's page 6, I believe, in English. It's para 10(b) -- sorry, page 7, 7 in English. Tasks are set here for the security organs. We see the heading in the original on the previous page, but we don't actually need it at this moment. You have seen this document more than once. Tell us more about your opinion on the assignment of tasks to take care or accommodate any prisoners of war that may be taken during this action and the tasks of the security organ related thereto.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I particularly analysed the tasks given to the security organ because it's set out in the objective, and in my report that was my job. I was somewhat surprised or nonplussed by the fact that security organs were designated to identify areas of collection, together with the military police, to determine the areas of collection of prisoners of war and war booty. In all my prior testimony, I continuously pointed out that it was not the job of security organs, it's not within their scope of work, not within their purview. On top of that comes the fact that all I said about threatening activities, we could see that the security organ had its hands full with the problems that were within its own purview, within its own scope of work, and they had a lot to do in keeping with the rule of the corps, which designates the security organ as responsible for all security affairs in the command and the primary organ responsible for counter-intelligence. So this assignment to the security organ is not consistent with its functional purpose, but it's also not consistent with the objectives of this operation, from the viewpoint of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How do you understand, in this paragraph, the term which says, sectors will be designed or determined? How do you understand this term "sector"? What is its meaning in the military terminology?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The definition of a sector is rather vague from the point of view of precision, so that I can say only that a sector is a rather vague area. It has to be denoted by something, by a name, by a feature, where it is situated, so one could reach the feature that is part of that sector. The sector is defined by the security organ and says what it comprises. The sector is only a task, and you have to say which sector it is in this particular document, the sector features here only for the purposes of giving a task and later on the sector is defined in greater details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, war booty is mentioned here. Could you please tell us whether there is a document, a norm regulating the work of the security organ? Is the war booty mentioned as such?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the security organs are concerned, there is no reference to either prisoners of war or war booty. There is a special provision about war booty and how to treat war booty. War booty is something that is part of the purview of the logistics. They have to deal with the war booty. This is beyond the scope of activities of the security organs and I would not be able to provide any specific answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also looked at another version of this same order for active combat. On its first page, you can see that this is copy number 3 of this order. However, there is another version of the same order, which is 1D382, and it is entitled, "Copy number 2." Did you ever compare these two versions of the -- of the order?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report, I have stated that I have compared these two texts and I was able to find some differences in them. On the page defining the task that we have just discussed, a correction has been made, which has not confirmed the task of the security organ such as was featured in the first copy, but, rather, the sector of the collection of prisoners of war was directly determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just wait a minute for the text to appear on the screen. This is on page 5 in the B/C/S version and the penultimate page in the English version. I believe that it is page number 6. Could you please go one page back in the English text? Go back to the previous page. Now we have it. Yes. Now, could you please continue? And I apologise for interrupting you. We were not able to follow your words without the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the second line from the top of the page where it says that the security organs and the military police, and let me not read any further. This has been crossed out with a felt-tip pen. And then on the margin, it says, the sector of where prisoners of war will be collected is Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, prisoners of war and war booty. That is something else added on top of the handwritten sentence but obviously the first sentence was about prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now my impression is that that is -- that this is lacking from the translation. I can't see it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's inside. It's not written in the margin like the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Satisfied with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now tell us, please, what is your position, what is your conclusion with regard to these corrections in the document that we are currently discussing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I've already spoken about the task of the security organs and their attitude towards prisoners of war in dealing with those issues, one can say here that what is written here is completely in accordance with the purview of command with regard to the prisoners of war, so it is within the purview of the command and not of the security organ. So my opinion would be that whoever corrected the text completely complied with the regulations in terms of the work of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 1D1294? 1D1294, yes. I see we don't have a translation, so could you please briefly tell us about this document? What is it about? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order for active combat, operative number 1 of the command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade issued on the 5th of July 1995. This order followed the order that we have just discussed. This is a document that regulates all the issues of the engagements of the Bratunac Brigade in the tasks given to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at the document to see how the security issues have been regulated by this document? This is on page 5 of this document, and I'm talking about providing security during combat. Look at item 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, did we get an English translation of that? I know there is one. It should be in e-court. We can give you a land on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't help you there. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the document is -- was translated but I cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Many years ago. And it's -- we'll get it up for you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have it in e-court? No. All right. We'll try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, if we can find it, we'll get it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Let's proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How does this document regulate the collection of prisoners of war and war booty or the issue thereof in more general terms?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a nutshell, the collection of prisoners of war and war booty is regulated just as in the item that we just discussed in the operative number 1, order for combat, by the command of the Drina Corps. What I'm saying is this: I'm not commenting upon the contents of this order but in terms of security, this order regulates obligations towards prisoners of war in the way as provided for by the handwritten corrections in felt-tip pen. That's how things were regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who issued this order? And you will find it on the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was issued by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document that we saw a little while ago, which is 1D382. Can we have page number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In meantime, I would just like to inform the Trial Chamber that the translation of previous document is marked as 5D01107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you verify that, Madam Registrar, please, or Prosecution? 1107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Prosecution 3025, too. Between those numbers, we ought to be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you have pointed our attention to, handwritten on the margin, there is another part of the text that has been crossed out. Could you please tell us what it is and whether it is also in keeping with the rules regulating the work of the security organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This thing that was first written and then crossed out is not in keeping with the rules of the security organ because the security regime in the areas of the units is established by the unit commanders, whereas the security organs propose measures that should be applied within the framework of the security regime. They should be implemented and their application should be controlled. This is something that commanders should order but something that is proposed for the commander's order or decision, depending on the type of command that is in place at the time. That is why there is no separate document as an instruction about the security regime. Rather, it is part of the order-issuing document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you are able to read the handwritten words on the margin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I can read is, "no, no" on both sides of the text. These are the only two words. There is no other comment provided next to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, based on the combat documents and all the other documents that you were able to peruse, would you be able to say whether in the course of the Operation Krivaja 95 or whatever this military operation should be called, there were any prisoners of war taken up to the moment when enclaves were separated and the objective of the operation was achieved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documentation that I perused, I could not find any traces or any information pointing to the fact that in the course of the realisation of Krivaja 95, there were any prisoners of war, and especially there were no such prisoners that would have been treated according to the items by the security organs. Not even according to this order that has not been drafted according to the rules of the work of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any documents providing information about the places where the military police of the Drina Corps were during the course of this operation, i.e. when this operation was planned and executed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came by a document which provides very precise information as to the situation, the deployment of the military police of the Drina Corps in the month of June. In a nutshell, this document provides information to the effect that 90 per cent of the military police were engaged in those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We are going to look at 1D1078.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1078.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When was this report compiled? Would you be able to tell from the stamp in the left-hand side corner?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report of the command of the 5th Battalion of the military police. It was drafted on the 7th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at item 5 or paragraph 5 in this document? Can we go to next page, please? We have the translation but we don't have the original second page. I can provide it to be shown on the ELMO. Let's look at item number 5 of this document. Tell me, please, when you look at item number 5, can you conclude that the unit or a large part of the military police of the Drina Corps was engaged in tasks which are not prescribed by the rules of service of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in this item that in the past month and since the report was drafted in the month of July, obviously the report refers to the month of June, 90 per cent of the unit was carrying out combat tasks in the zone of responsibility, according to this report, combat tasks were not military policing tasks. They were part of the combat activities of the units that were carried out in the area listed further on. I'm not going into the details of the geography. What matters is that this was combat and not the regular military policing duties, the mere fact that says it was beyond the scope of the activity of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just read the rest, where they were engaged until the full stop?

utterances.speaker: PETAR VUGA [Resumed]
